sections.h2: What does the Jefferson County Recorder of Deeds do?
sections.html:
The office keeps the public record of land transfers and ownership in Jefferson County, Missouri. It records deeds, deeds of trust, releases, easements, plats, restrictions, surveys and affidavits, and it issues marriage licenses (county page). Veterans' discharge papers (DD214) and tax liens can also be recorded on request.

  • Address: 729 Maple Street, Hillsboro, MO 63050.
  • Phone: 636-797-5414.
  • Cutoff: documents presented after 4:30 PM are held for processing on the next business day.
  • Rule: a document must be recorded in the county where the property sits. A Jefferson County office cannot record land in another county.

The office does not draft documents, supply blank forms or notarize the papers it records. The staff point owners to a title company or real estate attorney for that.

sections.h2: What does a deed need before the Jefferson County recorder will accept it?
sections.html:
The recorder follows section 59.310 of the Missouri statutes, which the county reprints on its recording requirements page. A document can be refused if it misses any of these points.

  • Pages printed on one side, not bound, on white or light paper of at least 20 pound weight, with type no smaller than 8 point in dark ink.
  • A blank top margin of 3 inches on page one for the recorder's stamp, and at least three-fourths of an inch on every other side.
  • On the first page below the margin: title, date, grantor names with marital status, grantee names, any statutory addresses, the legal description and any reference book and page.
  • A legal description such as lot, block and plat, or metes and bounds. A street address is never accepted as a legal description.
  • A notary acknowledgment with seal and signature, and a mailing address for at least one grantee.

A document that fails the format rules can still be recorded for an extra $25. Exempt categories include papers signed before January 1, 2002, military separation papers, documents signed outside the United States, certified copies and court judgments.

One Jefferson-specific step catches sellers of acreage. When the legal description covers less than 10 acres in an unincorporated area, or part of a lot in a subdivision, the county Planning and Zoning Department must exempt the transfer deed before the recorder will take it.

sections.h2: How much does it cost to record or copy a document in Jefferson County?
sections.html:
The state legislature sets recording fees, and the office prices a document by its page count. Fees must be paid before recording, by cash or by a check payable to the Jefferson County Recorder of Deeds. The county links a Real Estate Recording Fees PDF from its recorder quick links, so ask the office or your title company for the figure on your deed.

Recorder charges listed on Jefferson County pages
ItemCharge
Copy of a recorded document$2 first page, $1 each added page
Certification of a copy$1
Deed that fails the format rules$25 extra
Pay-per-search online records site$8.95 per search, $1 per page copied

Card orders by phone add a $1 processing fee from the card company plus postage. The county notes that part of every fee goes to the State Land Survey Office, which uses it to update state surveys and keep vital land records. That office also oversees registered surveyors.

sections.h2: What are the steps once a deed reaches the recorder?
sections.html:
The county describes a six-step path. Knowing it helps you judge why a closing package sometimes takes a day or two to come back.

  1. Staff check dates, signatures, name spellings and the acknowledgment.
  2. The document is accepted and priced by page count.
  3. It is stamped with date and time, given a document number and sealed on page one.
  4. It is scanned.
  5. It is indexed by grantor and grantee name.
  6. A second check confirms the index entry, and the document goes back to the address given. A self-addressed envelope speeds that return.

If a deed is rejected, the preparer gets it back with the reason. A deed being re-recorded must be re-acknowledged and must state why it is being re-recorded.

sections.h2: Which deed fits my Jefferson County sale or transfer?
sections.html:
The recorder's FAQ separates three common types. A warranty deed passes title to a buyer, with the seller promising the title carries no liens from the seller or earlier owners. A quit claim deed lets current owners add or remove an owner, change a name or fix an error. A beneficiary deed, also called a time of death deed, records the owner's intent for after death.

A deed of trust is the mortgage lien. Each new loan or refinance records a new one, and when it is paid the lender must record a deed of release that cites the original document number. A seller with an old, unreleased lien should ask the lender for that release before closing.

The recorder advises hiring an attorney or title company for any deed, and adds that an owner can make their own deed if it meets Missouri's formatting rules.

sections.h2: How do I search Jefferson County land records?
sections.html:
You can search in person at the vault index, which lists grantor (seller) and grantee (buyer) names alphabetically. Search your own name as grantee to find the deed from your purchase, then use the book and page number it gives. Online, the office points to a pay-per-search site, a Laredo subscription for records from April 1985 to the present, and the hosted COTT Systems site for older records.

Laredo needs a signed user agreement from the Recorder. A lost deed does not cancel ownership, since the recording is the primary evidence of title and a certified copy stands in for the original.

The county's recorder quick links also carry a Property Fraud Alert notice, a reasonable stop for any owner of a paid-off house who is approached about a deed transfer.

sections.h2: What is the Jefferson County housing base behind the recordings?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau lists 96,228 housing units and 88,309 households in Jefferson County, with about 2.58 people per household. The share of persons living in the same house a year earlier is 90.1%, a sign of long tenure (QuickFacts). Building permits totaled 617 in 2025, so new construction deeds enter the record steadily beside resales.

A sale of a house here often produces three recordings in a row: the seller's deed of release for the old loan, the warranty deed to the buyer and the buyer's new deed of trust. The office checks, prices by page count and indexes each document on its own, so a closing with several documents adds several entries to the grantor and grantee index. Ask your title company which documents it will present and in what order.

Communities that file documents here include Arnold, Festus, De Soto, Crystal City, Pevely, Herculaneum, Hillsboro and Byrnes Mill, with Eureka mostly on the St. Louis County side.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Jefferson County, Missouri?
faqs.a: At the Recorder of Deeds office, 729 Maple Street, Hillsboro. Call 636-797-5414 first. Anything handed in after 4:30 PM waits until the next business day.

faqs.q: Can the recorder write my deed for me?
faqs.a: No. The office cannot prepare documents or give legal advice, does not hand out blank forms and does not notarize papers it records. A title company or attorney handles that.

faqs.q: Is a street address enough for the legal description?
faqs.a: No. Section 59.310 requires a lot, block and plat, or a metes and bounds or section, township and range description. The address alone is not accepted.

faqs.q: What does a certified copy of my deed cost?
faqs.a: The county lists $2 for the first page and $1 for each added page, plus $1 to certify. A phone order by card carries a $1 card fee and postage.

faqs.q: Do I need planning approval before recording a deed for a small parcel?
faqs.a: Sometimes. A deed for under 10 acres in an unincorporated area, or part of a subdivision lot, needs a Planning and Zoning exemption before the recorder will take it.
